articles.title: US midterm elections 2026: Record number of hijabis elected to statewide and national offices
articles.description:
US midterm elections 2026: Record number of hijabis elected to statewide and national offices

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Yasmine El-Sabawi
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 16:04

        
      
    
      
    
                There's a distinct difference when an American lawmaker is so visibly Muslim, given the rampant Islamophobia across the country
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Georgia State Representative Ruwa Romman speaks as part of the 'No Kings' rallies at Love Park in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on 14 June 2025 (Lisa Lake/Getty Images via AFP)
                  Off
                  Tuesday's midterm elections saw a remarkable wave of firsts that may have been unthinkable if US President Donald Trump had not spurred such backlash across the country. 

Among them were victories for four state senators-elect and one US congresswoman who all wear the hijab - a record for the country, and certainly a stunning outcome given the rabid anti-Islam rhetoric and threats that have taken hold since the Trump administration swept to power in January 2025.

These are women whose appearance has been caricatured and insulted by corporate media, Republicans, and trolls online, thus putting a direct target on their backs. 

Last week, the Muslim Public Affairs Council (Mpac) expressed concern about the escalation of far-right, anti-Muslim provocateurs in the US, because their actions often result in calls for increased law enforcement presence, and could therefore have ended up dissuading Muslim Americans from voting at all. 

But while the turnout demographics are still being assessed, several visibly Muslim, young women have now risen to elected office to take matters into their own hands. 
  
    



  



All of them are progressive Democrats.

In Georgia, a relatively conservative southern state that just saw its first Jewish senator re-elected and the first-ever Black woman take the governor's office, state representative Ruwa Romman won her bid for the state senate.

She was already the first hijab-wearing Muslim in the state legislature. 

Romman rose to national prominence during the 2024 presidential election, when pro-Palestine Democrats pleaded with the Democratic National Committee and presidential candidate Kamala Harris to allow a Palestinian speaker at the party's convention. That request was denied. 

Romman, whose grandfather was born in Jerusalem, was meant to be that speaker. She had already been an elected official for two years by then. 

The Biden administration's wholesale support for Israel's assault in Gaza, now called a genocide by the United Nations and Holocaust scholars, ended up costing the Democrats support among young voters, and contributed to their demise at the ballot box. 

Calls for a ceasefire in Gaza

In New York, Aber Kawas will be headed to the state senate in January.
  
    



  



Like Romman, she is a Palestinian immigrant to the US, and told Middle East Eye earlier this year that she sees collective action and civic engagement in her adopted city as a path towards reconciliation.

Her undocumented father was arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the years after the 11 September 2001 attacks, when New York City and the country saw an aggressive crackdown on Muslims, and included FBI raids, disappearances, and mass surveillance across mosques and other institutions.

Kawas's father was held for nearly three years before he was deported to Jordan. So many of her childhood memories involve watching her distraught mother speak to her father through a pane of glass - in what she described as a "mixed-use" detention centre that also housed prisoners accused of criminal conduct, not just civil violations.

ICE's violent arrests in broad daylight and on public streets have shocked much of the country, leading to the Democratic "bluenami" in Tuesday's results. 

In Illinois, 27-year-old state representative Nabeela Syed faced stiffer competition from her Republican opponent, but won comfortably with 57 percent of the vote.  


  

  Aber Kawas becomes first Palestinian American elected to New York State Legislature
    Read More »


The Indian American was first appointed to the legislature to fill a vacant seat in 2022, and has made affordability and equity in healthcare a core component of her agenda.

She was recently endorsed by The Daily Herald, a 150-year-old newspaper that covers the greater Chicago area, as well as the storied Chicago Tribune.

Like Romman and Kawas, she has criticised Israel. One day after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel, she co-signed a letter along with several other Illinois lawmakers demanding that Washington enact a ceasefire.

Critics called the letter a defence of Hamas. 

“We will not be able to achieve peace when millions of Palestinians are denied basic human rights," the letter said. "We urge the United States and the international community to work toward long-term solutions that end the inequality that is at the root cause of the violence."

In Connecticut, state representative Maryam Khan, who has been in office since 2022, is moving on to the state senate in January after defeating her Republican opponent by a landslide. In her August primary, she unseated a Democratic incumbent who had served for nearly a decade. 

Khan, who was born in Pakistan, served as House Chair of the Select Committee on Special Education, as well as the judiciary and education committees, while in the state legislature.

State Senate Democratic Majority Leader Bob Duff welcomed Khan to the chamber on X, where he called her "a former special education teacher and a fighter for our kids". 
  
    



  



Earlier this year, Khan came under fire from Republicans for putting a Pakistani flag on her desk, after Pakistan helped broker the first post-war US-Iran talks towards a ceasefire.

“I displayed the Pakistani flag as a reflection of my heritage and personal pride. Any suggestion that it represents something improper or disloyal is simply inaccurate,” Khan told The Connecticut Mirror.

“Pakistan is a longstanding diplomatic partner of the United States, and acknowledging one’s background does not diminish commitment to this country or to serving the people of Connecticut.”

'Islamophobia was not a winning strategy'

Perhaps no one is as familiar with the weight of Republican backlash as Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, who was re-elected to the US Congress for the fifth time on Tuesday. 

In 2018, she became one of just four Muslims to ever serve in the House of Representatives in Washington, DC, and the only one to wear a hijab.

Since then, she has been a frequent target for Trump.



Just two weeks ago, federal agents from Homeland Security Investigations carried out a pre-dawn raid on Omar's home and confiscated her cell phone, laptop, and other devices.

Born in Somalia, she arrived in the US in 1995 as a child refugee, and obtained US citizenship at 17 after her now-deceased father was naturalised.


  

  US midterm elections 2026: Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim elected to Senate
    Read More »


The Department of Justice is reportedly looking into whether she was actually 18 at the time, meaning she would have had to apply for citizenship separately from her parents. 

Trump has repeatedly called for an investigation into whether she is a lawful citizen, and even claimed she married her own brother for immigration purposes. Omar has denied these allegations, but both the president and Vice President JD Vance have insisted for the past year that she should be investigated, and Trump has led chants of "send her back" at his rallies. 

The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed US officials, has reported that the administration is building a case to strip Omar of her citizenship and deport her. 

According to The Washington Post, nearly 100 Republican members of Congress have posted about Islam or Muslims on social media since the start of 2025, almost all of it negative, and several have called for Muslims to be deported.

In April, the Center for the Study of Organized Hate found that between February 2025 and March 2026, Republicans built "a coordinated anti-Muslim campaign involving 1,111 social media posts, eight bills, and a 62-member congressional caucus", and that many of the posts met all five criteria for speech likely to inspire violence.

Haris Tarin, vice president for policy and programming at Mpac, told MEE on Wednesday that the anti-Muslim climate that has been built up ultimately backfired. 

"Ilhan Omar won with higher margins than her previous elections, and you had multiple other Muslim women who were also elected who were visibly Muslim, so that showed that it did not work," he said.

"Islamophobia was not a winning strategy in this election cycle."

articles.title: US issues fresh sanctions against individuals and entities aiding Iran
articles.description:
US issues fresh sanctions against individuals and entities aiding Iran

    
    

        
    
                The US Treasury issued fresh sanctions on Wednesday targeting what it called "the vast criminal network" of companies and individuals tied to Iran.

It named Indian nationals Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, as well as two other Indian citizens who head two of the couple's businesses, and nine separate entities connected to Sharma.

"Their schemes have provided false flags and certifications to sanctioned vessels involved in transporting Iranian petroleum, including vessels operating on behalf of the Iranian military and its proxies," the department said in a statement.

The department also sanctioned Turkey-based Fugo Group Services Inc for its ongoing support of Iran's heavily sanctioned aviation sector.

articles.title: Gaza volunteer surgeon Adam Hamawy wins US House seat in New Jersey
articles.description:
Gaza volunteer surgeon Adam Hamawy wins US House seat in New Jersey

    
    

        
    
                Democrat Adam Hamawy, who treated Palestinians in Gaza during Israel’s genocide, has defeated Republican Gregg Mele to represent New Jersey’s 12th Congressional District.

The 57-year-old former US Army combat surgeon campaigned against military assistance to Israel and other countries committing human rights violations.

He has also condemned the war on Iran as “illegal and immoral”. In a May interview he accused Washington of “catering to special interests of the defense contractors and war mongers and with organizations like [American Israel Public Affairs Committee] AIPAC and Israel’s special interests.”

Hamawy joined missions to Gaza in 2024 and 2025 through the Palestinian American Medical Association, with coordination from the World Health Organization.

articles.title: Egyptian doctor who undertook medical missions to Gaza will now go to Congress
articles.description:
Egyptian doctor who undertook medical missions to Gaza will now go to Congress

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Mounira Elsamra
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 20:05

        
      
    
      
    
                Adam Hamawy's win in New Jersey makes him the first Muslim to represent the state in the House of Representatives
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Adam Hamawy speaks during an AFP interview after meetings at the White House and on Capitol Hill, in Washington DC, on 14 June 2024 (Drew Angerer/AFP)
                  Off
                  Egyptian-American surgeon Adam Hamawy has won his bid for Congress in New Jersey’s 12th congressional district, joining the blue wave across the US and making history as the first Muslim and Egyptian American to represent the state.

During his victory speech in the midterm elections on Tuesday, he spoke directly to the people in Gaza, saying: “To the men, women and children of Gaza and Palestine. Your smiles give me the courage and the hope to fight for a better world."

Republicans previously held the majority of the House of Representatives with 218 seats, four more than the Democrats at 215, but come January, Hamawy is one of the congressional wins to give his party a majority. with a whopping projected 250 seats, according to MS Now.

Middle East Eye attended Hamawy's watch party in Princeton, New Jersey, where he declared during his speech that he was ready to get to work and vowed to “hold Donald Trump accountable”.

“I'm a surgeon, and I can tell you that we are going to stop the bleeding. We are going to fight for every American that's been left behind by the establishment that has been ruling Washington for so long.”
  
    



  



Inside his party, the atmosphere was one of overwhelming solidarity. Congresswoman Bonnie Watson Colmen introduced Hamawy to the stage for his victory speech, embracing him. Jewish Voice for Peace members held signs that said “Jews for Hamawy.”

But that image of solidarity stood in harsh contrast to the reality that Hamawy faced throughout his campaign.

“I have never seen anti-Muslim hate as open and as loud, and as accepted as it is today, not just here in New Jersey, but across the country. It's always been there, but now it's open and allowed and vicious, and it's been targeted against my family, my coworkers, my friends. My loyalty and my patriotism have been questioned.”

Why Hamawy?

The watch party was stacked with keffiyeh-clad and American flag-wielding voters who came out to support him.

Yoshi, a New Jersey voter, says Hamawy's pro-Palestine stance resonated with him.

“When he decided to run for office, I saw that he was putting forward the message of ‘health care not bombs’ which spoke to me.” 


'Organised people can really beat organised money'

- Yoshi, New Jersey voter


Yoshi volunteered for the campaign and attributes Hamawy's win to grassroots efforts from the pro-Palestine community.

"Organised people can really beat organised money. A lot of people who I volunteered with had also organised during the Uncommitted New Jersey campaign,” he told Middle East Eye.

For Yoshi and others, Palestine is the political litmus test and politicians that pass get their vote. “Our work is not over; after Doctor Adam Hamawy wins this election, the work starts the next day. Because right now, Gaza is still under siege. Gaza is still being bombed. We don't want our taxpayer money to be spent on war and genocide anymore.”

However, it is precisely some of those stances that triggered attacks from pro-Israel and right-wing elements during his campaign, but Hamawy brushed them off. 

“I have done harder things” than mount a political campaign, Hamawy told MEE for an article before his primary election run.

“What’s the worst thing they’re going to do? Call me some names, attack me? I have seen much worse.”

In May of this year, The Wall Street Journal ran an opinion article linking Hamawy’s values to those of convicted Muslim cleric Omar Abdel Rahman, commonly known as the “Blind Sheikh”.
  
    



  



In what was then the largest terrorism trial ever to take place on US soil, Abdel Rahman was found guilty in 1995 of planning to kill former Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak during his visit to the United Nations headquarters.

He was sentenced to life in prison and died in 2017.

Among the 200 witnesses who testified at that trial was Hamawy himself, who told the jury that while the cleric did convey anti-American sentiment, he did not expressly spell out how a murder would be carried out. 

But a member of the New Jersey Education Association, Nancy Sedlak, told MEE that Hamawy's win renews her faith in American politics, away from all the nastiness that took place during the campaign.

“I can finally breathe a little bit and relax a little bit. It's been a horrific ten years, and it's hope that we can reclaim our democracy.”

She says she voted for Hamawy because she hopes he can help “bring back the middle class” and  “appreciates his concern and support for public education”. 

Who is Hamawy?

Hamawy, a US Army veteran and surgeon, ran a campaign focused on economic justice and working-class priorities, promising Medicare for all, affordable housing and education, stronger protections for immigrants and civil liberties, and a US foreign policy rooted in human rights rather than endless war. He touted the slogan, “health care not bombs.”  


  

  Egyptian-born doctor and Gaza volunteer wins New Jersey Democratic primary
    Read More »


Hamawy was raised in New Jersey by Egyptian immigrant parents, joining the New Jersey Army National Guard to serve his country and pay for college. He went on his first humanitarian medical mission when he was a medical student in war-torn Bosnia.

After the 9/11 attacks in New York City, Hamawy treated victims at Ground Zero.

Just three years later, he served in the US Army as a combat trauma surgeon, saving the life of Illinois Senator Tammy Buckworth.

Over the last 30 years, Hamawy has volunteered as a doctor in disaster and war zones, including Sudan, Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, Turkey, and Jordan, to name a few. He volunteered as a physician in Gaza during the height of Israel’s genocide in 2024 and 2025, providing medical care to Palestinians amid the collapse of the territory’s healthcare system.

Come January, Hamawy will take his fight for the working class and against wars to DC - in the halls of Congress.

articles.title: The Democrats' midterm election sweep breaks the internet
articles.description:
The Democrats' midterm election sweep breaks the internet 

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Nouran Saleh
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 19:22

        
      
    
      
    
                Democrats secure majorities in both chambers of Congress in the US midterm elections, prompting celebrations across social media
                      
                  
                  

  


                  US Senator-elect James Talarico speaks during a midterm election night event at the Long Center for the Performing Arts on 3 November 2026 in Austin, Texas (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/AFP).
                  Off
                  In a sweeping victory, the Democratic Party won majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the US midterm elections on Tuesday.

The results marked a remarkable political shift, with Democrats flipping several key states, most notably Texas, where James Talarico won his Senate race, marking the first Democratic statewide victory in 30 years.

Other notable states include North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, and Kansas. 

The Senate races also saw a series of historic firsts, including Michigan electing its first Muslim senator, Abdul El-Sayed; New Hampshire electing its first openly gay senator, Chris Pappas; and Minnesota electing Peggy Flanagan as its first Native American woman senator.

“first disabled” “first black woman” “first latina” “first openly gay man” “first latino” “first palestinian” “first black man” “first muslim” “first native american” “first trans woman” pic.twitter.com/WZlAepJlJG— The Notorious J.O.V. (@whotfisjovana) November 4, 2026 



The historic firsts extended to the gubernatorial races, where Democrats secured 28 governorships compared with 20 for Republicans. New Mexico elected its first Native American governor, Deb Haaland, while Texas elected Gina Hinojosa as its first Latina governor. Wisconsin also elected its first Black governor, David Crowley.

“first black woman senator in US history”“first openly gay man elected to US senate”“first latina governor in Texas history”“first native american woman governor in US history”“first black governor in Wisconson history”WOKE IS BACK pic.twitter.com/oDeMoyWSBY— mils ✩˚.⋆ (@thelorebitch) November 4, 2026 

The results sparked widespread reactions online, with people taking to social media to celebrate the Democrats’ victory.

Last night was a great time to be here pic.twitter.com/cJ5xwdP79V— Ruff Criminal (@RuffCrim) November 4, 2026 

Memes and reactions flooded social media, with many describing the Democratic sweep as a blue tsunami or "Bluenami", referring to the number of states that turned blue after years of Republican dominance. Others declared that "woke is back".

WE ARE SO BACK, SO WOKE AND SO BLUE pic.twitter.com/bpIOVC9JAX— mils ✩˚.⋆ (@thelorebitch) November 4, 2026 

Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan was among the night's most widely discussed results. He defeated Republican candidate Mike Rogers following a highly contentious and closely watched race, during which Sayed faced Islamophobic and racist attacks.

Abdul El-Sayed outperformed Kamala, Biden, Hillary, and Slotkin in a swing state by running on Medicare for All and being framed as the anti-Israel candidate.There’s a lesson to be learned here!— A Left-Wing Account ™️ (@PushDemsLeft) November 4, 2026 

People worldwide have joined the online celebrations, while others are now looking ahead to what the Democrats will do with their newly secured majorities.

Amid the celebrations, many have also used the results to remind voters that every vote counts.

articles.title: UK: Dozens arrested outside Supreme Court hearing on Palestine Action ban
articles.description:
UK: Dozens arrested outside Supreme Court hearing on Palestine Action ban 

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Areeb Ullah
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 17:30

        
      
    
      
    
                Lawyers representing the co-founder of Palestine Action said the group follows the traditions of the Suffragette movement
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Dozens of activists, including Jewish activists, and celebrities faced arrest on first-day of last ditch appeal against ban on the direct-action group (Reuters)
                  Off
                  Lawyers representing the co-founder of Palestine Action have argued that the direct-action group has never advocated for violence against individuals as the campaign to overturn its designation as a terrorist organisation by the UK government reached the Supreme Court.

Speaking on the first day of the two-day hearing, Raza Husain KC, representing Huda Ammori, opened proceedings and said that less than one percent of the group’s protests met the legal definition of terrorism.

"It’s not the label that's important – it’s the substance. Palestine Action has never advocated violence against individuals and follow a similar vein to the Suffragettes who were not peaceful... are part of the tradition [and] proven right by history and venerated.

“The uncontroverted evidence shows moreover that [the] Suffragettes, anti-war groups, environmental groups, animal rights protesters all used tactics similar to or more extreme than Palestine Action, yet they were not regarded as terrorists or proscribed,” said Husain.

The barrister noted that the Suffragettes are now widely celebrated despite using tactics like arson and bomb attacks in the cause of campaigning for the right to vote for women.
  
    



  



Ammori’s legal team also emphasised that the ban on Palestine Action had impacted the group’s right to freedom of speech and protest, noting that it had created a “chilling effect” on British society.

“Filton marked a watershed moment - [the activists] were arrested as terrorists and treated as such,” said Husain.

“That came as a shock to the movement.”

The Supreme Court hearing comes after judges granted an appeal following the government's successful proscription under anti-terrorism laws.

It marks the final attempt for the group to appeal the ban after going through several courts to reach this stage.

Outside the court, dozens of activists risked arrest for holding signs that quoted posts from Sarah Helm, former journalist and wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, who caused an uproar after publicly criticising the ban on Palestine Action.

Last month, Helm posted “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” after books by Irish author Sally Rooney were withdrawn from sale in the UK because of her support for the group.
  
    



  



Protesters customised the signs by swapping out “authors” for descriptors that reflected their personal identities or professions - including “Jew”, “physiotherapists”, “son of a Holocaust survivor”, “gardeners” or “normal people”.

Among 25 people who were arrested by the police for holding the placards are actor Alfie Enoch, who starred in the Harry Potter movies, and Massive Attack musician Robert Del Naja.

articles.title: Aipac and the Michigan Senate race: How the Israel lobby became toxic
Americans voted against war. The Democrats must not mistake that for a mandate
articles.description:
Americans voted against war. The Democrats must not mistake that for a mandate

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Omar Suleiman
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 17:20

        
      
    
      
    
                Midterms showed that political power can be challenged, even when backed by extraordinary wealth. But can this movement be channelled towards global peace?
                      
                  
                  

  


                  US Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer takes questions in Washington, DC, on 4 November 2026, after historic Democratic midterm victories (Tom Brenner/Getty Images/AFP)
                  Off
                  The American political establishment is about to learn a dangerous lesson from the wrong interpretation of a historic election.

On Tuesday night, voters delivered a devastating rebuke to US President Donald Trump and his cronies, handing Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in the process. 

Candidates who challenged the political consensus around Israel, Gaza and Iran achieved victories that would have seemed unimaginable only a few years ago. 

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), long treated as an almost untouchable force in American electoral politics, watched candidates it opposed prevail, despite extraordinary spending. Association with Aipac and pro-Israel lobbying groups is now a liability. 

And before Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries congratulate themselves, they should understand something: the voters who made these victories possible did not vote for them and their Democratic establishment. In fact, they voted against it.
  
    



  



This was not simply a Democratic wave; it was a revolt against a political order that has made endless war a bipartisan commitment, Palestinian suffering an acceptable cost of doing business in the Middle East, and American taxpayers unwilling financiers of destruction abroad, while their own communities struggle at home with all sorts of avoidable challenges.

The results were not exclusively a referendum on foreign policy. Americans also voted against rising living costs, corruption and an increasingly unpopular president. 

But the Gaza genocide and the Iran war, launched at Israel’s behest, were no longer peripheral issues that candidates could safely avoid. They became part of a larger reckoning over what American power is being used for, who benefits from it, and who is expected to pay the price.

Historic victory

The question now is whether the Democratic Party will recognise that shift, or attempt to absorb the energy of an antiwar movement while preserving the very policies that made such a movement necessary. With the history of the Democratic Party, most of us aren’t holding our breath.

Abdul El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, defeated Republican Mike Rogers after surviving one of the most aggressive campaigns against a candidate in recent memory.

His victory was historic, of course. But reducing it to a milestone of religious representation would miss its political significance.

According to the Associated Press news agency, Aipac spent nearly $30m opposing him during the Democratic primary. Its preferred candidate, Representative Haley Stevens, lost.


The Democratic establishment cannot credibly present itself as the innocent beneficiary of public outrage. It helped create that outrage


Then, just two days before the election, Stevens endorsed Sayed’s Republican opponent, Rogers. After months of bitter disagreement over Israel and sabotaging her former opponent, she decided that defeating the Democratic nominee was preferable to accepting the direction Michigan voters had chosen.

It was an extraordinary exposure of the priorities operating within the party’s establishment.

Even though Schumer and others in the establishment leadership condemned the latest move by Stevens, and supported Sayed in Tuesday’s election, they had almost all backed Stevens during the primary, and were timid in their acceptance of Sayed even before the Stevens stunt. The establishment ultimately rallied behind the nominee only after voters had rejected its preferred choice.

The party leadership should not be allowed to rewrite the story as though it had enthusiastically nurtured the very movement it initially attempted to defeat.

Michigan voters were told, in effect, that a candidate willing to challenge unconditional support for Israel was too risky, too divisive and too far outside the political mainstream.

They elected him anyway. And Michigan was hardly alone. In Maine, Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins after openly criticising Israel’s conduct in Gaza and opposing unconditional American military assistance.
  
    



  



In Texas, James Talarico, who has spoken of his opposition to the Gaza slaughter from the perspective of a Christian and former teacher, won a Senate seat that Democrats had been unable to capture for more than three decades.

Framework shattered

Now, I want to say this clearly: I don’t believe any of these candidates have gone nearly as far as they should have in openly calling out Israel’s criminality, without somewhat pandering to the liberal Zionists stuck in the current Democratic ranks. But they have all gone further than what was typically acceptable in the political order.

And these candidates are not ideologically identical, nor did every Democratic victor campaign against Aipac. But their victories demonstrate that unconditional support for Israeli military policy is no longer the prerequisite for political viability that Washington once assumed.

The old threats are losing some of their power.


  

  Aipac and the Michigan Senate race: How the Israel lobby became toxic
    Read More »


For decades, American politicians were conditioned to speak about Israel in a narrow vocabulary. Security was legitimate. Palestinian freedom was controversial.

The genocide in Gaza has shattered much of that framework. Americans watched hospitals destroyed, children pulled from rubble, journalists killed, and families displaced repeatedly. They watched their government continue supplying weapons, while insisting that it was working tirelessly for peace.

Under former President Joe Biden, the Democratic administration helped to sustain Israel’s military campaign, even as outrage grew over Palestinian civilian deaths. Under Trump, the Republican administration embraced further military escalation and deepened the regional catastrophe. Same garbage, different pile: that’s how many of us felt.

This is why the Democratic establishment cannot credibly present itself as the innocent beneficiary of public outrage. It helped create that outrage.

And the shift was visible well before election night. Polling reported by Al Jazeera in August showed substantial opposition to continued military aid to Israel among Democratic voters in early presidential primary states.

The distance between the party’s leadership and its voters has become impossible to ignore.

Moral rupture

The Israel lobby’s problem is therefore bigger than a series of electoral defeats. Its political brand has become increasingly associated with a foreign policy that many Americans no longer wish to defend.

That does not mean the organisation has lost its money, access or influence. It means those resources no longer guarantee political obedience.

And that is an important beginning. Gaza was the moral rupture, and the war on Iran widened the political reckoning.

  
  
      



    Abdul El-Sayed and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, take the stage after he won the Michigan Senate race, in Detroit, on 4 November 2026 (Jeff Kowalsky/AFP)
  




  
    



  











For years, Americans were told that each new military escalation in the Middle East would make them safer. Each intervention came with assurances of strategic necessity, limited objectives and eventual stability.

Yet Americans have watched the same repeated cycle, over and over again: military escalation, civilian suffering, regional instability, enormous public expenditures, and promises that the next use of force will finally deliver security.

The war on Iran just brought that contradiction home, especially for “America Firsters” who felt betrayed.

Voters facing rising prices and economic uncertainty were once again being asked to accept the costs of another foreign war. The administration that promised to put America first was consumed by military confrontation abroad.

Schumer and Jeffries may soon hold extraordinary institutional power. But the Democratic leadership’s record on Israel gives little reason to assume that electoral victory will produce meaningful change in that party.

Opportunities squandered

In April, Schumer was among a small minority of Senate Democrats who opposed resolutions seeking to block certain weapons sales to Israel. In July, Jeffries voted against ending American military aid, even as a substantial portion of his caucus supported the measure.

These were opportunities to use congressional power to challenge the material support sustaining Israeli military operations, and they squandered it again.

The leadership chose continuity, and now it will have fewer excuses. The problem is not that the Democratic Party lacks the means to pursue a different policy. It is that too many of its leaders have lacked the willingness to exercise a moral backbone. 


A true antiwar movement must be willing to support candidates who uphold those commitments, and challenge those who abandon them, no matter what party they come from


The deeper question is whether this election represents a temporary protest against Trump, or the beginning of a lasting transformation of American politics. I hope it is the latter, but I am very sceptical.

The US does not simply need Democrats who are more articulate in condemning Republican wars, while remaining willing to finance wars of their own. It needs a political movement that understands opposition to war as a governing principle, rather than a campaign slogan. That means opposing illegal and unnecessary military interventions, regardless of which party occupies the White House.

It means applying international law consistently, whether the accused government is an American adversary or a so-called ally.

It means challenging the military-industrial complex and the enormous political incentives that make war profitable for some, while catastrophic for millions.

And it means building an economic vision that recognises the connection between militarism abroad and neglected needs at home.

The path forward

A true antiwar movement must be willing to support candidates who uphold those commitments and challenge those who abandon them, no matter what party they come from. It must also refuse to disappear once the election is over.

Because the political establishment has a familiar way of surviving popular revolts. It adopts their language, celebrates their victories, and then quietly restores the policies that produced the revolt in the first place.

The Democrats cannot be permitted to do that with Gaza as it continues to bleed, as the genocide started and was sustained on their watch. They cannot be permitted to do that with this stupid war on Iran and what follows.

There is much to celebrate about Tuesday’s election, with some of the worst actors in modern political history being sent packing.


  

  Can Iran war deadlock be broken at the US ballot box?
    Read More »


Candidates who were told they could not win without submitting to the old foreign policy consensus proved otherwise. Communities that had been dismissed as politically expendable demonstrated their electoral power. A lobbying establishment accustomed to intimidating dissent discovered that voters could reject its preferred candidates.

Aipac’s defeats should not become merely another chapter in the Democratic Party’s comeback story. They should mark the beginning of the end of a bipartisan consensus that has wreaked havoc on so many innocent lives with our tax dollars for too many years to count.

If Schumer and Jeffries interpret this election as permission to restore the old order, they will have misunderstood the moment. If the antiwar movement interprets it as proof that its work is finished, it will have misunderstood the struggle. And if they return to business as usual, they should understand that they can lose their own primaries next time around.

The American people have demonstrated that political power can be challenged, even when backed by extraordinary wealth and institutional influence.

The next question is whether that power can be redirected towards peace.

The voters have opened a door that the political establishment spent decades trying to keep shut. Now the US needs an antiwar movement strong enough to make sure it never closes again.

articles.title: Dapo Akande elected as ICJ judge, restoring British presence inside highest UN court
articles.description:
Dapo Akande elected as ICJ judge, restoring British presence inside highest UN court

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Sondos Asem
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 12:19

        
      
    
      
    
                Oxford professor argued against annexation of Palestinian territory and challenged Britain’s legal positions on Chagos, Iraq and Syria
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Dapo Akande addresses the International Court of Justice on behalf of Japan during hearings on Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory, in The Hague on 22 February, 2024 (UN Photo/ICJ-CIJ/Frank van Beek)
                  Off
                  British international lawyer Dapo Akande has been elected to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), restoring a British presence on the United Nations’ highest court after almost a decade.

Akande was elected judge on Tuesday alongside France’s Francois Alabrune, Singapore’s Rena Lee, Jordan’s Mahmoud Daifallah Hmoud and Kenya’s Phoebe Okowa. Nine candidates contested the five seats. 

Their nine-year terms begin on 6 February 2027. Hmoud and Okowa, already serving after elections to fill vacancies, secured full terms.

As a lawyer and scholar, Akande has helped advance arguments on proving genocide and the illegality of annexing Palestinian territory, and he is expected to sit on the bench as the court decides on the ongoing case brought by South Africa accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention in Gaza.

Akande, Oxford’s Chichele Professor of Public International Law and a member of the UN International Law Commission, will become the first British judge on the court since 2018.
  
    



  



The British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband welcomed the election as "a victory for the UK’s commitment to the rule of law and our ability to stand up for our values on the world stage".

Akande describes himself as a “generalist public international lawyer”, whose work spans armed conflict, international criminal law, human rights, international organisations and the settlement of disputes between states.

“Dapo is a careful, nuanced jurist and a precise and effective communicator,” said Janina Dill, Akande’s co-director of the Oxford Institute for Ethics, Law, and Armed Conflict.

“As a colleague I have most admired his even keel and wisdom. I am glad the court can benefit from these qualities at this moment in time," she told Middle East Eye after Akande's election.

Candidates needed an absolute majority in separate votes in the General Assembly and Security Council, 97 votes and eight votes respectively. The council’s permanent members have no veto in judicial elections.

The court’s judges serve independently of their governments. 

Based in The Hague, the ICJ settles disputes between states and issues authoritative advisory opinions. Unlike the International Criminal Court (ICC), it determines state responsibility and does not prosecute individuals.
  
    



  



Its judgments in disputes are binding on the parties, although enforcement can depend on action by states and a politically divided Security Council.

Previous ICJ interventions

Akande’s election comes as the ICJ prepares to issue a judgment in The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar over atrocities against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority. Akande served as counsel for Britain in this case as part of the UK’s legal team alongside Alison Macdonald KC and Naomi Hart.


  

  The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide
    Read More »


In this case, Britain intervened jointly with Canada, Denmark, France, Germany and the Netherlands to present arguments about interpreting the Genocide Convention.

Their submissions warned against making proof of genocidal intent so demanding that findings become practically impossible.

The states also argued that genocide encompasses acts beyond killing, including sexual violence and the imposition of destructive living conditions. Children’s particular vulnerabilities must inform assessments of serious harm, deprivation and displacement, they added.

The Myanmar case, in which judgment is scheduled for 19 November, has become a focus of US attacks on the court.

Last month, US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz accused the Gambia's ad hoc judge, who is the latest Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay of seeking to lower the threshold for proving genocide so it could be used against American and allied soldiers.


'If elected, I will decide cases on the basis of a faithful and impartial application of the law'

- Dapo Akande, newly elected ICJ judge


Waltz warned that Washington would be “watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely”, invoking US sanctions against the ICC.

Akande has also addressed the ICJ on Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory, appearing for Japan during the court’s advisory opinion proceedings on the illegality of Israel’s occupation. 

Akande argued that a state could not get around the ban on taking land by force simply by never formally announcing it had annexed it.

He told the judges that moving populations, seizing land, evicting residents, building long-term infrastructure and exploiting natural resources such as water could amount to annexation in practice, especially when officials described those changes as permanent.

He also argued that a state could not keep territory it had seized by claiming self-defence. Self-defence allowed a country to protect land it already had, not to gain more, he said, adding: “Permanent annexation can never be a proportionate response to an armed attack.”

Criticism of UK positions

Despite British support for his candidacy, Akande has previously challenged London’s positions before the court.

In the 2018 hearings on the Chagos Islands, which Britain separated from Mauritius before the Indian Ocean island became independent, he appeared for Zambia to rebut the UK's arguments.

Britain had argued that the matter was a territorial dispute between it and Mauritius, and that the court should not rule on it without British consent. Akande rejected that, telling the judges: “This case is about the international law obligations regarding decolonisation.”


  

  Who is Phoebe Okowa? The newly elected ICJ judge and her opinions on Israel-Palestine
    Read More »


He argued that the right of colonised peoples to decide their own future, known under international law as self-determination, concerned all countries, not just the two involved.

He also challenged Britain’s argument that this right was not yet part of international law in 1965, when Chagos was separated from Mauritius.

To make the point, he cited Britain’s own statements from that period accepting that all peoples had that right.

His criticism of British legal arguments has also extended to military action in the Middle East.

In an April 2018 opinion commissioned by then Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, Akande rejected the government’s justification for air strikes against Syria's Assad government.

Akande described its position as “significantly flawed”, concluding: “The military action taken was not in accordance with the United Nations Charter and international law.”

He argued that international law did not recognise the unilateral right of humanitarian intervention claimed by Britain. Even if such a right existed, he said, the strikes did not appear to meet the government’s own conditions.

Akande has also argued against the UK's participation in the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

In 2010, he led a group of academics in a submission to the Iraq Inquiry challenging the legal case for the invasion.
  
    



  



The government had argued that the Security Council’s 1990 authorisation to use force against Iraq, after it invaded Kuwait, could be revived more than a decade later because Iraq had breached the terms of the 1991 ceasefire. The submission called this “an untenable interpretation of the UN Charter”.

The submission also argued that even if the argument held, the UN Security Council’s resolution of November 2002 did not meet its conditions, so the attorney general, Lord Goldsmith, had been wrong to conclude the invasion was lawful.

In his statement as an ICJ candidate, Akande emphasised legal rigour, cooperation across legal traditions and judicial independence.

"If elected, I will decide cases on the basis of a faithful and impartial application of the law having listened carefully to the arguments of participants in the proceedings," he wrote.

articles.title: UK government facing legal challenge over IHRA antisemitism definition in schools
articles.description:
UK government facing legal challenge over IHRA antisemitism definition in schools

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Oscar Rickett
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 13:30

        
      
    
      
    
                The Good Law Project and British Jewish group Na'amod tell MEE contested IHRA definition protects Israel, not Jewish students
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Police officers intervene as a pro-Israel banner is held during a rally in London on 16 November 2024 (AFP)
                  Off
                  The British government is being challenged legally over its recommendation for schools to adopt the contested IHRA definition of antisemitism.

The Good Law Project launched a legal challenge against the government on Monday. The group’s executive director Jo Maugham told Middle East Eye he was worried that “rules which conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism… could be among the drivers of antisemitism”. 

“Antisemitism and the rise of antisemitism in Britain and around the world are very real things, and I want to say to British Jews who are at the sharp end, I hear your pain,” Maugham said.

“But I also worry - and it's a point I've made many times - that rules which conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism, and that unjustifiably constrain the freedom properly and vigorously to criticise Israel, could be amongst the drivers of antisemitism.”

The UK Department of Education’s move to encourage schools to adopt the IHRA definition follows the recommendation made in British education official and academic David Bell's recently published report on antisemitism in the country's schools and colleges.
  
    



  



The Bell report has been questioned for misrepresenting its findings, equating criticism of Israel with antisemitism, and surveying small numbers of students from a narrow age bracket.

The controversy surrounding the IHRA’s working definition of antisemitism, which was originally formulated in 2004 as a non-legally binding tool to assist in monitoring antisemitism, comes mainly from the fact that seven of its 11 “illustrations” of antisemitism include references to Israel.


'Jewish pupils should be safe at school, and antisemitism has to be taken seriously. The IHRA definition doesn’t do that job'

- Na'amod


The definition’s lead author, Kenneth Stern, has warned against its use as a disciplinary or legal instrument, arguing that it may risk restricting legitimate political expression.

In 2018, leading human rights lawyer Geoffrey Robertson issued a legal opinion stating that the definition is “likely in practice to chill free speech” by encouraging complaints against legitimate criticism of Israel.

The British Jewish group Na’amod, which also opposes the imposition of the IHRA definition, told MEE: “Jewish pupils should be safe at school, and antisemitism has to be taken seriously. The IHRA definition doesn’t do that job.”

“Its examples run criticism of Israel together with hatred of Jews, and in universities it has overwhelmingly been used to censor speech about Israel rather than to protect Jews,” a spokesperson for the group added.

“In schools, that leaves teachers policing children who talk about Gaza or the Nakba, instead of tackling real anti-Jewish racism. It also fails Jewish pupils, many of whom don’t tie their Jewishness to support for the Israeli state.”

The Bell review

The IHRA definition has been formally adopted by 47 countries.

Its adoption in British schools was one of 27 recommendations made in the Bell review. Following its publication on 21 October, it was widely reported that “three in five” Jewish students had experienced antisemitism in English schools.

This figure came from a survey of 5,000 students, 92 of whom were Jews aged, between 16 and 18. Seventy of those students responded to a question about whether they had personally experienced or witnessed antisemitism, with 29 of them - 41 percent, or around “two in five” rather than “three in five” - saying they had.


  

  UK antisemitism report found increase in 'anti-Israel' sentiment, not 'anti-Jewish' attitudes
    Read More »


The Bell review itself acknowledged that this was a “low sample size” and should be “treated with caution”. It also found that “anti-Jewish attitudes are typically less prevalent and have remained more stable, whereas anti-Israel sentiments are more prevalent and have been increasing”.

Middle East Eye asked the UK Department for Education about its plans to adopt the IHRA definition and about whether it had considered the warnings - including from the definition’s lead author - about the “chilling effect” the definition can have on pro-Palestinian expression and criticism of Israel.

“Antisemitism is a growing problem across society, including in our schools and colleges, and Jewish children and staff should never face hatred or prejudice in education,” a Department for Education spokesperson said in response.

“That is why we have accepted all 27 of Sir David Bell’s recommendations and are acting on them, including encouraging schools and colleges to adopt the IHRA working definition of antisemitism.

“The IHRA definition has been adopted by 47 countries and countless public bodies and can provide a practical framework for teachers and pupils, and help give greater clarity on how to identify and tackle antisemitism wherever it occurs.”

'Consistency is what we want'

Bell’s review recommends separate measures for tackling anti-Jewish hatred, distinct from existing anti-racism and anti-bullying policies. The National Education Union has criticised the move, warning it risks “creating a hierarchy of racism”.

The Good Law Project and Na’amod both told MEE that the British government should be consistent in how it deals with racism and not apply special treatment to antisemitism.


'It is not merely important to protect the space to advance vigorous criticisms of Israel’s appalling actions. We think it is necessary in a moral society'

- Jo Maugham, Good Law Project


“What we really want is for government to be consistent in how it tackles hate speech,” Maugham said. 

“The rules that apply to one minoritised group should also be the rules that are applied to other minoritised groups… Consistency is what we want.”

“Antisemitism should not be taught as exceptional,” the spokesperson for Na’amod said. “It should be taught alongside racism and Islamophobia, because these struggles are bound together and the people who fight one are the natural allies of those who fight the others.

“Treating antisemitism as a special case with its own rulebook prevents that learning and sets Jewish safety apart from everyone else’s.”

Gary Spedding, a cross-party political consultant on Israel-Palestine, told MEE he thought Bell’s review was “sloppy, misleading and inaccurate”, and that it was part of a “systemic, legal and institutional dismantling of any support for Palestine, or any education and discussion about Palestinian history and existence within the UK education system”.

Pro-Israel influence in British schools

Over the past decade, the Department for Education and British government ministers have issued warnings to headteachers, teaching staff and local authorities over how Palestine is approached in schools.

These interventions have often come after lobbying from pro-Israel groups such as UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI), the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Community Security Trust (CST).


'Palestine is viewed as a partisan issue triggering school neutrality, but Zionism and Israel are not'

- Gary Spedding, political consultant on Israel-Palestine


In 2021, the BBC removed a seven-part series of educational videos about Palestine from its GCSE Bitesize platform - a free classroom resource for teachers - following pressure from UKLFI. 

Former Conservative education secretaries Gavin Williamson and Gillian Keegan both formally instructed headteachers to ensure “political impartiality” when it came to discussions on Israel-Palestine in schools. 

“Palestine is viewed as a partisan issue triggering school neutrality, but Zionism and Israel are not,” Spedding told MEE. “Meanwhile, the activities of pro-Israel advocacy organisations, operating in and having access to UK schools, do not receive an equivalent level of UK government or institutional scrutiny,” he said. 

A plethora of pro-Israel groups, including StandWithUs UK, United Jewish Israel Appeal and JNF UK provide educational resources, speakers and trips to Israel for British students and teachers.

StandWithUs has said that it helps students “stand strong in the face of antisemitism and anti-Zionism”, while the JNF allows them to “explore Israel” and offers “workshops on Zionist history”.

“Israel advocacy organisations try to argue their presence in the school system is necessary to counter rising antisemitism and anti-Zionism in schools,” Spedding said.

“But our educational unions have noted that the resulting imbalance leaves teachers highly anxious about covering topics related to Palestine, answering pupils’ questions and queries with regard to Palestine, and that traditional pro-Israel and Zionist viewpoints go largely unscrutinised by the UK government.”

“It is not merely important to protect the space to advance vigorous criticisms of Israel’s appalling actions,” Maugham reiterated. “We think it is necessary in a moral society.”
